solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Protective cover from university book penned by Mr Fitzgerald? (8)

indicators.note: something penned is shut inside a pen, so B sits inside the letters around it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, held between M and R

annotation.surface: A dust jacket written by some Mr Fitzgerald for a university book.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: 'Mr Fitzgerald' reads as one man, but MR is just letters and Fitzgerald is Ella, very much not a Mr.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: the thing you hold over your head to keep off rain or sun.

entries.clue: In France, one pegs out lingerie? (6)

blocks.note: to peg out is slang for to die

annotation.surface: A French woman hanging her lingerie on the washing line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pegs out' paints clothes pegged on a line; its slang sense, to die, is the one wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Undies is the informal word for underwear, and lingerie is the dressier word for women's underwear.

entries.clue: Criminal, overcome by temptation, first to nab diamonds (6)

indicators.note: the letters are swamped by BAIT, which closes around them
takes only the opening letter of nab

annotation.surface: A thief who could not resist and went straight for the diamonds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Overcome by temptation' reads as the criminal giving in; it actually says the two letters are smothered by the bait.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bandit is a robber, usually armed, one kind of criminal.

entries.clue: Botch an overdue attempt (9)

indicators.note: to botch is to mess something up, so the letters come out wrong

annotation.surface: Someone making a mess of a long-delayed try.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Botch' looks like a verb acting on the attempt, but it only scrambles the two words after it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, noun for noun: to make an endeavour is to make an attempt.

entries.clue: Entering name, put down 4 into 501 — boy grasps one way to solve it (4,8)

indicators.note: to enter is to go into, so the name letter goes into LOG
in its placing sense, putting one thing inside another: IV inside DI
to grasp is to hold in the hand, so SON closes around I

blocks.note: to log is to record, put down in writing

annotation.surface: A sum set out: record the answer when you divide 501 by 4.
annotation.walkthrough: '4 into 501' is itself a division sum, and 'it' points back to that sum, so the definition leans on the wordplay. The '4' is a number, not a cross-reference to 4 down.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: long division is the pencil-and-paper method you would use to work out 501 divided by 4.

entries.clue: Tough bird with clipped wings back from vet (6)

indicators.note: a bird's wings are its sides, so both end letters are cut
takes the rear letter of vet

blocks.note: OSTRICH without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A hardy bird recovering from a wing clip at the vet's.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wings' suits a bird literally, but here it means the word's two ends. The bird is the ostrich, which fittingly cannot fly anyway.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of firm and unbending: a tough line on discipline is a strict one.

entries.clue: The bags I failed to open — one rustles? (5)

indicators.note: to bag is to capture, so THE holds I
takes the opening letter of failed

annotation.surface: Someone who couldn't get the bags open, the plastic still rustling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rustles' suggests the noise of bags; its other sense is stealing livestock, which is what a rustler does.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a rustler steals cattle or horses, so one who rustles is a particular kind of thief.

entries.clue: Removed papers, keeping notes in order (8)

indicators.note: to keep is to hold on to, so ID holds the notes inside it

blocks.note: sol-fa notes so, la, te, which follow one another up the scale

annotation.surface: Someone clearing away papers while keeping their notes sorted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In order' is not an anagram signal: so, la, te really are consecutive on the do-re-mi scale.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of remote: a removed or isolated village is cut off from others.

entries.clue: Picked up skill with pen, capturing very English caricature (8)

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting ART reads it bottom to top, TRA
to capture is to take prisoner, so TRA and STY together close round VE

annotation.surface: A cartoonist who picked up the knack of drawing a very English caricature.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pen' sits beside 'skill' as if it were a drawing tool; it is an animal enclosure.
annotation.definitionFit: A close synonym: both a travesty and a caricature are distorted, mocking imitations of the real thing.

entries.clue: Appreciate cuddling new puppy involves mid-morning tussle (4-4)

indicators.note: to cuddle is to wrap your arms round, so DIG hugs N inside it
to involve is to include, so DOG takes N inside it
takes the central letter of morning

blocks.note: slang: I dig it, I appreciate it
a puppy is a young dog
the middle letter of morning, inside DOG

annotation.surface: A morning playfight while someone enjoys cuddling a new puppy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mid-morning' reads as a time of day, but it supplies the fourth of morning's seven letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal use: a ding-dong is a heated row or scrap, named for the clanging back and forth.

entries.clue: Aims to get hammered, gulping second cocktail (6)

indicators.note: letters beaten out of shape, MISA
to gulp is to swallow, so the rearranged letters take MO inside

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, inside MI SA

annotation.surface: Someone setting out to get drunk, downing a second cocktail.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinking scene is the disguise: 'hammered' means drunk on the surface and shuffled in the wordplay, and 'second' is not the next drink but MO.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the mimosa is one particular cocktail, champagne with orange juice.

entries.clue: Bobby Kennedy’s final meeting with former European publishing operation? (4-3-5)

indicators.note: takes the closing letter of Kennedy

blocks.note: a bobby is a British policeman

annotation.surface: Robert Kennedy's last meeting, with a former European press baron.
annotation.walkthrough: Bobby Kennedy was a real politician, but here 'Bobby' is a British policeman, COP. The question mark admits that copy-and-paste is only loosely a publishing operation.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose definition by example: duplicating text with copy-and-paste is a routine editing step in getting material into print.

entries.clue: Carbon in atmosphere brought about by energy plant (5)

indicators.note: read as placement, carbon sits in the atmosphere, so C goes inside AIR
turned about, so AIR with C in it runs backwards

annotation.surface: Carbon in the atmosphere being produced by an energy plant.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about power stations and emissions, so 'plant' reads as a factory. It is the definition, and a garden one.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: Erica is the botanical name for heaths and heathers, one kind of plant.

entries.clue: Support for opener that takes catch? (9)

annotation.definition: Support for opener that takes catch?

blocks.note: the surface reads a cricket opener, the first batsman; the setter means a door, and the frame holds it up
a catch dismisses a batsman; here it is the door's latch, which the frame receives

annotation.surface: A cricket question: what backs up the opening batsman who gets caught?
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket the opener is the first batsman and a catch gets him out; read domestically, every word describes a door frame instead.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight once opener means door: the frame supports the door and takes its latch.

entries.clue: Repetitive band churning out the same material? (8,4)

annotation.definition: Repetitive band churning out the same material?

blocks.note: the surface reads a pop group stuck in a rut; the setter means a band of rubber going round and round
not identical songs but identical products carried off a production line

annotation.surface: A dull pop group that keeps releasing identical songs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'material' suggest musicians and their songs; both words have factory senses that fit the answer exactly.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight in the factory sense: a conveyor belt is a looping band that carries mass-produced goods.

entries.clue: Mountain guide’s tale following conclusion of film — gather round (6,3)

indicators.note: takes the closing letter of film
in its sense of surrounding, REAP goes around the rest

blocks.note: to harvest, placed around LIE F M

annotation.surface: A mountain guide telling a story as the film ends, the group gathering round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a joining word, but it is the abbreviation F. The 's stands for 'is', linking definition and wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful definition: a relief map shows the rise and fall of the land, so it guides you to where the mountains are.

entries.clue: Mentally unsettle treacherous spy chief, exposed (5,3)

indicators.note: treacherous things are not what they seem, so the letters of spy turn

blocks.note: revealed, as in the secret is out

annotation.surface: A double agent's spymaster being unmasked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spy chief' reads as one person, but it splits into two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal phrasal verb: to psych someone out is to undermine their nerve, playing on the psyche, the mind.

entries.clue: Arrives, grabbing tea behind motorway rest facility (8)

indicators.note: to grab is to seize, so ARR holds the rest inside it
in its sense of coming after, so CHAI is placed after M

blocks.note: British motorways are numbered M1, M25

annotation.surface: Someone pulling up behind a motorway service station for a cup of tea.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rest facility' wants to be a motorway services; it is simply a chair you rest in.
annotation.definitionFit: A whimsical description: an armchair is furniture provided for resting in.

entries.clue: Unusually rude about parking next to building (12)

indicators.note: in its sense of around, so SURLY goes round the rest

annotation.surface: An unusually rude remark about the parking by some building.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' looks like an anagram signal pointing at 'rude', but it is the definition. 'Building' is a verb, not a structure.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, adverb for adverb: unusually warm and surprisingly warm say the same.

entries.clue: Retreat from rough edge that hurts! (6)

blocks.note: a burr is the rough ridge left on cut metal

annotation.surface: Someone flinching back from a sharp edge that caught them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' reads as a verb, but the answer is the noun: an animal's hideaway.
annotation.definitionFit: Retreat as a noun means a hideaway, and a burrow is the one a rabbit or fox digs.

entries.clue: Yes, given shake-up within country, many leaving in spring (6)

indicators.note: the letters of yes are shaken into a new order
the result goes inside GER
MANY departs from GERMANY

annotation.surface: A shake-up in some country, with many people emigrating in springtime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season people leave in; it is a hot spring, and 'many' is taken literally out of GERMANY.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a geyser is a hot spring that shoots water into the air, like Old Faithful.

entries.clue: Delighted (with) arrangement of straw, a bear retires (4-1-4)

annotation.definitionNote: the bracketed 'with' marks that cock-a-hoop is usually followed by 'with' or 'about'

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so POOH reads backwards

blocks.note: a cock is a small conical heap of hay or straw

annotation.surface: Someone thrilled with a straw arrangement as a bear goes to bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arrangement' is not an anagram signal here: a cock (haycock) is a heap of straw. The bear is Winnie-the-Pooh.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to be cock-a-hoop is to be jubilant, and like delighted it often takes 'with'.

entries.clue: Something used in pool to check temperature is crucial (5)

indicators.note: to check is to hold back, so A CUE holds T in

blocks.note: a cue, used to strike the balls in pool

annotation.surface: A thermometer used in a swimming pool, where checking the water temperature matters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pool' suggests a swimming pool and 'temperature' the water; it is the table game, and the thing used is a cue.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of critical: an acute or crucial shortage is one at its most serious point.

entries.clue: Musical piece regularly felt subdued (5)

indicators.note: takes letters at regular intervals, every second one

annotation.surface: A piece of music that left someone feeling low each time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Felt subdued' reads as a mood; it is only a letter source.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: an étude is a study, a short piece written to practise one technique.

entries.clue: In Spain, what comes after work? Answer’s unclear (6)

indicators.note: in its sense of following in sequence, so QUE is placed after OP and A

annotation.surface: A Spaniard asking what happens after work and getting a vague reply.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Comes after work' sounds like the evening; it only places QUE after OP. The 's stands for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: something opaque lets no light through, so an opaque answer is one you cannot see into.

entries.clue: Old basilica no longer minted coins (8)

blocks.note: St Mark's, the great basilica in Venice

annotation.surface: An ancient basilica that no longer produces its own money.
annotation.walkthrough: The ostmark was the currency of East Germany, withdrawn in 1990.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical definition: East Germany's currency vanished at reunification, so ostmarks are coins nobody mints any more.

entries.clue: Cutting encircles boundaries of granite quarry (6)

indicators.note: to encircle is to form a ring around, so TART surrounds GE
the outside letters of granite

blocks.note: first and last letters of granite

annotation.surface: Stone-cutting going on around the edges of a granite quarry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quarry' belongs with granite and cutting as a stone pit; it means the hunted prey.
annotation.definitionFit: The hunting sense: quarry is the animal being pursued, the thing aimed at.

entries.clue: Military might consider holding a prisoner attached to Resistance (3,5)

indicators.note: SEE holds A POW inside it
to attach is to fasten on, so R is joined to the end

blocks.note: as in I'll see about it

annotation.surface: An army that might think about holding a captured Resistance fighter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Military might' reads as an army that might do something; 'might' is a noun meaning strength.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a navy's reach is one form of military strength.
